document.title: Answer of Constellation Energy Generation, LLC in Opposition to the Indicated PJM Transmission Owners' Motion for Extension of Time

BEFORE THE 
FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION 
PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., et al. 
 
 
Large Loads Co-Located at Generating Facilities

     v.

ANSWER OF CONSTELLATION ENERGY GENERATION, LLC 
IN OPPOSITION TO THE INDICATED PJM TRANSMISSION OWNERS’ 
MOTION FOR EXTENSION OF TIME 
Constellation respectfully opposes1 the Indicated Transmission Owners’ motion to delay 
compliance2 with the Commission’s order establishing rules to promptly interconnect large loads 
in the PJM region.3 The TOs seek a thirty (30) day extension of time for submission of 
(i) compliance filings due 60 days from the date of the order; and (ii) initial and reply briefs in the 
paper hearing that the Commission established in the December Order.4 The Commission should 
deny the TO’s Motion for three reasons.   
 
1 Constellation Energy Generation, LLC (“Constellation”) files this answer pursuant to Rule 213 of the Commission’s 
Rules of Practice and Procedure. See 18 C.F.R. § 385.213. 
2 Motion for Extension of Time, Shortened Answer Period, and Request for Expedited Action of the Indicated PJM 
Transmission Owners in the above-captioned proceedings (filed January 14, 2026) (the “TO’s Motion”). 
3 Per PJM Interconnection. L.L.C., 193 FERC ¶ 61,217, at Ordering Clause (C) (2025) (“December Order”) the 
applicable tariff revisions are due 60 days from the December Order, or February 16, 2026.  
4 TO’s Motion at n. 12: “currently initial briefs are due on or before February 16, 2026 with responses to initial briefs 
due March 18, 2026, and the replies to those responses due April 17, 2026. Under the 30-day extension, initial briefs 
would be due on March 18, 2026, responses to initial briefs would be due on April 17, 2026, and the replies to those 
responses would be due May 18, 2026.”

2 
First, the Commission’s 60-day deadline was appropriate in the circumstances given the 
national imperative to facilitate the prompt interconnection of large loads and the long delays in 
doing so in PJM. The Commission’s timeline is consistent with the Secretary of Energy’s proposed 
ANOPR and the Secretary’s statement that the interconnection of large loads to the transmission 
system—the subject of both the ANOPR and this show cause proceeding—“is an urgent issue that 
requires prompt attention.”5 The Commission’s compliance deadlines require timely action to 
break the logjam on serving these critical large loads. 
Second, the TO’s interest in delaying compliance is troubling in light of positions 
Commonwealth Edison Company (“ComEd”)6 has taken in Illinois where ComEd asserts that its 
rates need not reflect the new Commission-mandated transmission services because these are not 
yet final and unappealable.7 ComEd’s approach would simply ignore the current circumstance, 
which is that the Commission has found the existing rate structure where there is only a single, 
gross wholesale transmission rate to be unjust and unreasonable and directed replacement rates. 
Among other things, the replacement rates include a new class of interruptible or non-firm 
wholesale transmission service which, in turn, could reduce collateral and deposit requirements to 
take service from ComEd. The TOs’ attempts to delay compliance in the Commission’s docket 
 
5 On October 23, 2025, the Secretary of Energy proposed an ANOPR under section 403 of the Department of Energy 
Organization Act, 42 U.S.C. § 7173(a).  U.S. Department of Energy, Secretary of Energy, Letter to FERC re: 
“Ensuring the Timely and Orderly Interconnection of Large Loads,” Advance Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (Oct. 
23, 2025) (issued pursuant to Department of Energy Organization Act § 403, 42 U.S.C. § 7173) (cover letter, 
“Secretary’s Letter,” and Advanced Notice of Proposed Rulemaking, “ANOPR”); see Secretary’s Letter at 1. 
6 ComEd’s parent, Exelon, joined the TO’s Motion. 
7 ComEd Response to the Constellation’s Motion To Reopen The Evidentiary Record in IL ICC Docket Nos. 25-0677 
and 25-0679, p. 6 (Jan. 8, 2026) (“[t]he proposed retail tariff ensures that large load customers contribute revenue in 
accordance with their load requests … regardless of any changes FERC might or might not make to the design of 
transmission rates applicable to any particular transmission customer.”) (“ComEd January 8 Response”).

3 
thus are consistent with their efforts to avoid updating their rate structures until there is a final 
Commission order. Such delays are contrary to the December Order8 and the Federal Power Act.9   
Finally, prompt compliance in this proceeding in PJM is also critical because the record 
reflects that Transmission Owners have long benefited by delaying existing large load co-location 
requests unless customers agree in advance to take both transmission and distribution service from 
them.10 The TO’s Motion now seeks further delay.   
For all the above reasons, Constellation opposes the TO’s Motion. The Commission should 
deny the motion and continue with the deadlines as established in the December Order.   
 
 
8 See News Release, FERC Directs Nation’s Largest Grid Operator to Create New Rules to Embrace Innovation and 
Protect Consumers, (Dec. 18, 2025) available at https://www.ferc.gov/news-events/news/ferc-directs-nations-
largest-grid-operator-create-new-rules-embrace-innovation-and (“As technology leaps forward, clear and fair 
regulations must keep pace to support advancement, help prevent price volatility, and promote competition, 
ultimately benefiting consumers by keeping electricity costs manageable.”); see also  December Order, 
Commissioner Rosner Concurring (“a business-as-usual approach to load growth—planning for generation and load 
separately—will not suffice to timely meet growing demand while also keeping prices reasonable. Today’s order 
helps break the logjam.”). 
9 See 16 U.S.C. § 825l(c) (providing that the filing of an application for rehearing shall not, unless specifically ordered 
by the Commission, operate as a stay of the Commission’s order). In ComEd’s January 8 Response, ComEd alleges 
that until the Commission issues an order on compliance, “no actionable framework is in effect.” ComEd January 8 
Response at p.6. ComEd is incorrect. Unless and until the December Order is set aside, it is a final order that binds 
PJM, the TOs, and other market participants unless and until the Commission or a court of appeals determines 
otherwise.    
10 See Constellation Complaint at 6-9 (citing Protest of Constellation Energy Generation, LLC, Docket No. EL24-
149-000, Exh. 2 (correspondence with Exelon) (filed Oct. 30, 2024); Motion to Lodge of Constellation Energy 
Generation, LLC, Docket No. EL24-149-000, Exh. 1 (November 12, 2024 Exelon Letter) (filed Nov. 18, 2024)); 
see also Constellation Complaint, Exh. 5, Declaration of James R. McCoskey (detailing interaction with Exelon to 
study co-location projects); see also Atl. City Elec. Co., 190 FERC ¶ 61,109 (2025) (rejecting Exelon Transmission 
Owners’ attempt to force all co-located load to take full transmission service).
